The number of devices infected by the Kimwolf botnet at its peak,
reported by Synthient
, is somewhere over 2 million (primarily Android TV boxes). In an equivalently-sized infected fleet of TVs serving AI models, if every group of 15 TVs ran a copy of Gemma4-26B-A4B, we would have ~133k copies (“replicas”). A group of TVs like the ones in our demo can serve 2 agents simultaneously at roughly 0.3 tokens per second each, yielding 80k tokens/s across the botnet.
As a reference point, an H100 can serve Gemma4-26B-A4B at ~1.95k tok/s at
high concurrency with speculative decoding
, so our swarm would have at most about 40 H100s-worth of inference. This is a tiny amount of compute in absolute terms, and the agents are slow replicators (over 1-2 days per 9B replication). As an analogy, imagine the replicator as a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies, which replicate over days.
This is a rough estimate, as it’s anchored on a single class of IoT hardware and a single past botnet instance, but describes what a simple replicator released in the near future might look like. In practice, more capable replicators would take advantage of other types of low-security compute, and would be opportunistic about deploying models of various sizes on different devices. (It also wouldn’t have to load a model payload onto every device it compromises). Over time, we expect the amount of deployed edge compute to continue growing, while the minimum model size required for reliable replication falls.
D. Adaptation and uplift
Learning on the job
The “Adaptation” part of ARA is one reason why an AI replicator might outperform a traditional worm. Specifically, models and prompts can undergo Lamarckian evolution as they spread–that is, parent instances can pass on their prompts, code, and notes to their daughter replicators. In order to adapt and spread across a wide variety of hardware, a model would require two things:
Being above a certain threshold of capability for spreading onto a novel, unseen piece of hardware (or software environment, or network type).
Once seen, adapting to the type of environment it has landed in (it should replicate more reliably on hardware it has seen before).
Sections A and B test the first condition, and in the experiment below we test the second. Each Qwen3.5-9B instance keeps brief notes on the strategies it tried and the failures it encountered, before a new instance inherits those notes and attempts the same inference setup again.
Inference setup success rate across six generations of Qwen3.5-9B, each inheriting the former’s notes. Faint lines are the 20 individual lineages, and the bold line is the proportion of runs in each generation that complete setup. It rises from 45% in the first generation to between 61% and 84% in later ones. This uses the Memento setup (Appendix A).
Taking advice
Another concern is that small models can ask for help from a
frontier advisor
, a stronger model that is either offered as a tool call or gives unsolicited advice when the small model is stuck. To test this, we gave Qwen3.5-9B access to Opus 4.8 during the inference setup task. The frontier model’s advice doesn’t measurably help: small models tend to not know the right questions to ask, and they don’t improve when the advice comes unprompted.
Even when trained through reinforcement learning to use the advisor in a similar setting (Python coding problems), the small model still struggles to ask for help productively for inference standup. Both results are shown in the plot below.
Inference setup success rate by advisor access, with Wilson 95% intervals. Access to an advisor, whether offered as a tool call or given to the model automatically when stuck, gives no significant improvement. The two RL groups were trained with advisor access on software engineering tasks, and the rightmost group also rewards calling the advisor when stuck.
Since small models are capable and persistent individual agents and make poor use of advice, we think coordination is more likely to happen with a large model handling high-level strategy and spinning up small models as subagents.
E. How is this different from a pre-AI botnet?
Hard-coded botnets like the
Kimwolf botnet
each target a specific type of device – in Kimwolf’s case, Android TVs and mobile devices. An AI botnet isn’t tied to any particular hardware or software type, as evidenced by small models being able to set up inference engines on machines from a Jetson Nano to a Mac (see the table in section A). We expect AI botnets to infect more than IoT devices, and to use weight-based replication as just one strategy in their playbook. AI botnets could also act intelligently to counter defenders, but we haven’t tested this.
F. Blue-team mitigations
As with an epidemic, defense involves driving R₀ (the number of new devices each infected device goes on to infect) below 1, such that the replicator dies out instead of staying endemic.
Some elements around this threat model are in the defenders’ favor:
A weight-based replicator multiplying through IoT machines at scale would leave a network signature, visible as an anomaly in ISP flow-based monitoring systems. Newly infected hosts may receive multi-gigabyte model payloads from other devices or external hosting services, while distributed inference can produce sustained device-to-device traffic between machines that wouldn’t ordinarily communicate at that volume. Propagation itself would add additional scanning and outbound connection patterns.
In practice, the replicator trades off between replication speed and stealth: the faster it replicates, the more traffic it produces. Once the replicator is discovered, defenders can use honeypots (decoy devices) to collect the replicator’s harness and payload to characterize its behavior.
Remediation of the Mirai botnet
was possible
when an ISP used externally obtained infection evidence to quarantine and notify customers. Quarantining infected subscribers involved restricting their networks to only being capable of reaching a short whitelist of sites, and otherwise redirecting their browsers to cleanup instructions. This cleared 92% of infections within 14 days, against 74% with no notification. We’d expect quarantining to be similarly effective for an initial defense against a weight-based replicator. Eliminating the replicator completely would mean coordinating across every ISP with an infected network, which is difficult.
Manufacturers can shrink the pool of targets, with regulation acting to coordinate. For example,
default IoT passwords are now non-compliant in UK markets
. Moving to more secure defaults and raising the baseline for compliance will help harden against both AI and scripted botnets.
G. Conclusion: Signs of life
The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication. Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms. We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves).
At the same time, increasing amounts of inference compute are now available both inside and outside of datacenters (see Appendix D). It’s uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take. It could be a slow, distributed “digital slime mold,” living on relatively insecure compute. It could also be a powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.
As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control. While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute. The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves. We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.
Appendix
A. The Memento harness
Memento executes as follows:
We spawn an agent instance, which tackles the problem for a while (until generation timeout).
The instance keeps brief notes, and after timeout summarizes a small doc of the strategies it tried, the failures it encountered, and its performance (if successful).
We create a new agent instance that inherits the codebase and environment from its predecessor as well as the notebook.
In the serving experiment, each model is placed in a Memento harness and is given a 1.5 hour per iteration / 6 hour total timeout. Around ~1k tokens of information, including specs about the hardware and a script for a simple sample profiler, are given in the prompt.
Memento is intended to improve long-horizon reliability rather than grant new cyber or inference-specific capabilities. It’s also not a universally strong harness; we expect that small models will improve as replicators even without any harnessing as capabilities improve.
Single attempt compared against Memento, by model (95% Wilson CI).
B. Why pipeline parallel?
Common parallelism schemes for inference include tensor parallel (TP), expert parallel (EP), and data parallel. Most smart TV / IoT devices use ARM Cortex CPUs and DDR3/4 memory; on such machines, we’re almost always bandwidth bound.
We use pipeline parallelism for its fault-tolerant properties. As noted in (
Borzunov et al. 2022
), the failure of a single node in tensor parallel / expert parallel brings down the full set of machines running the model replica. Pipeline parallel allows the downed node to be replaced, with the KV cache for the layers held by the node recomputable via another forward pass of the node prior to the restarted node.
C. Throughput and memory on IoT hardware
Across such machines, we’re almost always RAM-bandwidth bound per-box across prefill and decode. Even on modest ARM-cortex cores, compute throughput outpaces RAM bandwidth. Decode workloads have significant per-machine idle time due to pipeline bubbling, as only one machine is active at a time during each forward pass. Concurrency with staggered work is possible, but tight memory constraints mean that concurrency stays low.
Per-box memory vs context — 4-bit weights + fp8 KV + activations.
Both prefill and decode tokens/s strictly decrease with sequence length. Below is a graph of our inference speeds against context length:
There’s also a minimum sequence length at which models are competent. The harness we use is forked off of the Pi coding agent (
pi.dev
) and contains a native compaction mechanism - even still, we find that models take a large performance hit when their sequence lengths are restricted below 32K.
Qwen3.5-9B agentic competence on the inference setup task vs. context window budget.
Given the above eval, we assume that a 32k context length may be sufficient for reasonable agentic performance. A standard 32k-length context window in our inference setup workload consists of 12–15% generated decode tokens, with the rest being prefill from prompts and toolcalls. Prefill tokens are much faster to compute by a factor of ~15, due to the pipeline bubbling. Taking the sum of time per token over the whole 32k context (taking into account prefill and decode speeds), we find that generating the 3.8-4.8k decode output tokens and processing the ~28k prefill tokens takes between 27.3-31.8h for Gemma4-26B-A4B and 10.9h for Qwen3.5-9B.
Per-chain output tokens (summed over a chain’s generations), by model; medians ≈ 19.7k / 12.3k / 11.0k. Data from the inference setup eval.
D. Edge Accelerators
We can compute a better upper bound by using the pool of Nvidia Jetsons, which are edge accelerators. Unlike the traditional IoT botnet, IoT edge devices can serve a full model wholesale. A Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB
runs Qwen3-30B-A3B
at 76.7 tokens per second, and an AGX Thor reaches 226 tok/s. Note that we don’t believe they’re unusually vulnerable - this is just to count the upper bound. The types of devices with Jetsons in the wild include:
AI-enabled smart cameras for security with embedded accelerators are deployed at substantial scale.
Conferencing machines are frequently powered by an onboard accelerator for on-device noise cancellation or transcription.
Vehicles, robot quadrupeds and bipeds, and drones. We expect cybersecurity to be a focal point for vehicles, so the majority of the potential targets likely lie in the other two categories.
At least one accelerator-equipped smart camera host appears to be reachable on IPv4 on a quick search on FOFA:
A FOFA search surfaces a host with a known edge accelerator, discoverable and answering HTTP 200 over IPv4. The fact that it’s accessible doesn’t mean it’s necessarily exploitable, though.
While it’s difficult to estimate how many edge-accelerator-equipped machines in the wild are reachable and vulnerable, we can calculate a strict upper bound of the amount of devices present. Across the wild there are on the order of 90 distinct NVIDIA-silicon IoT product lines and roughly 9.5 million fielded units. Reachability is overwhelmingly through outbound cloud-management tunnels instead of inbound ports, meaning that the majority are not web-reachable. There have been no historical mass-compromises of accelerator-equipped edge devices the way there have been standard IoT botnets, suggesting that compromise of such devices would be more difficult.
Fielded units per device family, colored by internet reachability.
A very rough estimate based on product data suggests that somewhere between 9,000 and 35,000 H100-equivalents of compute exist in edge accelerators, but the amount that’s reachable is likely an order of magnitude or more lower (and the vulnerable population even lower than that).
Aside
Aside from these edge accelerators, we also consider the small-business and industrial IoT tiers, such as NAS boxes, mini-PCs, and Rockchip-containing SoCs (like Orange Pis). Historically, we know small business NAS machines are vulnerable to ransomware and cryptojacking (
Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and National Cyber Security Centre 2020
), with each having 512MB-2GB of soldered RAM (which puts them in a similar category as the smart TVs). Mini-PCs are typically significantly more hardened, and machines like Orange Pis are capable (see our inference setup table) but are also difficult to breach.
Read more
E. Spearphishing capability
We also measure how proficient modern small models are at spearphishing. Spearphishing is the act of sending targeted messages to specific individuals to trick them into revealing credentials or running a piece of malware. While the agentic cyber capability of small models has skyrocketed, their general knowledge and linguistic sophistication have improved more slowly; we expect social engineering attacks and phishing to be largely accomplished by large/frontier models (although it’s very plausible that this is a secondary replication vector in a heterogeneous botnet running both large and small models).
Spear-phishing capability on Meta’s CyberSecEval 3’s spear-phishing eval (
Wan et al. 2024
), replicated locally. Scored on a scale of 0-5, with gpt-4o as a judge. Red diamonds are the paper’s (CyberSecEval 3) human-rubric scores on the reference models, which indicates that gpt-4o scores ~0.4-0.7 pts more leniently than human raters. 2 is “poor”, 3 is “intermediate”, and 4 “good.” When normalized to human raters, small models score “very poor” to “poor”.
The 405B reference slot uses Hermes-3-405B as a minimal-refusal stand-in for the unavailable Llama3.1-405B-Instruct.
F. Propagation with scripted inference setup:
We run a few more experiments on a network of 17 hosts in a topology like so:
Two networks with 8 hosts each, connected by a single node with access to both subnets. Each network is all-to-all connected. The worm agent begins on a single patient zero node in segment A; the pivot node adds a slight extra challenge in having the worm needing to gain access to the pivot node and re-scan from it.
Each is running Android with an ADB port open without authentication. Upon spreading to a new target, the agent is able to invoke a direct call to replicate itself immediately - this is just to measure the difficulty of the remaining steps, after we exclude the cyber and inference setup steps. As shown in the graph, even a 3B model reaches about half the nodes. This puts a bound on the number of blockers in our eval that we fail to measure under the cyber or inference setup elements.
A more detailed breakdown of the runs in “replication across a 17 node network.” Each column is the median number of nodes reached under different amounts of guidance in the prompt, and the subscript denotes how many agents cross over the pivot node to the other side of the network.

news.title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
news.content:
Policy
Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
Oct 14, 2026
Earlier this year, we shared an
update on our election safeguards
, which described how we measure and prevent political bias, detect misuse, and direct people to accurate voting information.
Below, we outline how we've built on that work and continued to strengthen our election safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.
How people use Claude for elections and politics
Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. That starts with understanding how people actually use Claude in these contexts. To do this, we used Anthropic Insights to develop a new analysis of 250,000 conversations over the course of a recent one-week period.
Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy, or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app. This includes people turning to Claude to follow the news, conduct academic or professional research on public policy, learn about candidates, and navigate government services. About 0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting. As we get closer to Election Day, we expect the share of political and election-related queries to
increase
This sample suggests people rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for. These kinds of requests showed up in about 0.01% of US Claude conversations. More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our
election integrity policies
were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations.
How many US Claude.ai conversations touch on politics, are about elections, or ask Claude whom or what to vote for.
Each dot represents 1 in every 10,000 conversations in a random sample of about 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026, which Claude classified using
a privacy-preserving method
. Because requests for a recommendation on whom or what to vote for are so rare, we show the upper end of a 95% confidence interval for that group. Examples are illustrative only. Most of the requests we see are informational in nature. People turn to Claude to make sense of geopolitical events, research candidates, draft documents, assist with coursework, and weigh arguments for and against policies.
What people ask Claude for in political conversations.
Conversations were clustered in a privacy-preserving, bottom-up manner through
Connecting people to trusted sources
Ahead of Election Day, we've added two ways for people to get reliable information directly in their conversations with Claude. As we shared in April, when people ask Claude.ai about voter registration, polling places, or election dates, we’ll continue to display a banner linking to TurboVote, a nonpartisan resource from
Democracy Works
Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the US. Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place will now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation. These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources.
Official voting information presented by Democracy Works.
Additionally, Claude will begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow, so that when people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation.
Measuring and preventing political bias
When people ask Claude about politics, they should get accurate and evenhanded answers that don't favor any particular political viewpoint. That’s why we test our models extensively for political bias before every model launch. Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are our most evenhanded to date, scoring 99% on our
political evenhandedness evaluation
Our latest models also engage more readily with political discussions and decline fewer requests, so people can get the information they came for. We're continuing to refine these evaluations, and also looking beyond them for new ways to pressure-test how our models handle political topics.
As part of that effort, we asked three independent groups to review how Claude handles free expression, each from a different angle with different methodologies.
The Future of Free Speech
, an independent think tank at Vanderbilt University, tested Claude on hundreds of requests on contentious topics, and the
Foundation for American Innovation
compared how Claude responded to matched prompts from the left and right, ranging from mainstream policy debates to more extreme scenarios. On both of these evaluations, most of the responses were rated as strong, engaging substantively with requests. The
Collective Intelligence Project
surveyed more than 2,000 people in the US, UK, and India in developing an evaluation. Through a three-stage process, participants proposed principles for handling sensitive topics, ranging from health to politics, identified topics to test, and helped develop criteria for judging model responses. CIP synthesized this input and tested for agreement across demographic and cultural groups to establish shared principles.
These evaluations also identified areas where Claude still falls short. The Future of Free Speech and the Collective Intelligence Project both found that Claude rarely refused requests, but sometimes added unsolicited caveats and counterarguments, such as inserting an opposing view into an advocacy email. And the Foundation for American Innovation found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t always hedge evenly, and was more likely to soften arguments for right-leaning positions.
We're addressing this in a few ways. We've improved how Claude responds to direct yes-or-no questions and requests for shorter answers, where we found its answers could be less balanced. We're also using these findings to improve when and how Claude adds caveats or counterarguments, so it treats requests from across the political spectrum more consistently. And we're continuing to improve how we test for uneven hedging, building on existing evaluations that use matched prompts from the left and right. More broadly, we're working to expand our political bias evaluations to better reflect real conversations and to cover candidates and voting questions as well as policy issues.
How we define misuse
Our
Usage Policy
prohibits using Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections, from spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, to impersonating election officials or trying to suppress turnout. Each year, we update the policy to reflect our models’ evolving capabilities and feedback from our customers. This year’s update, which we
announced
last week, clarifies what our election rules cover and what they don't, and adds new examples to help people understand where the lines fall.
We know many political campaigns use Claude for legitimate, everyday tasks, so we recently
published a guide
to help them understand where these policies apply. It covers the many ways campaigns can put Claude to work, such as drafting press statements and fundraising emails, prepping for debates, analyzing turnout data, and building voter outreach materials. It also spells out what’s prohibited, such as using Claude to create fake social media profiles that pose as real people, mass-producing comments to inflate a campaign’s engagement, or writing content for news sites and pages that falsely claim to be independent.
Testing and strengthening our defenses
We deploy automated classifiers that are trained to detect election-related abuse. To see how these safeguards hold up in practice, we partnered with the
Institute for Strategic Dialogue
(ISD) and the
McCain Institute
, both independent research organizations, to pressure-test our protections in the US, Israel, and Brazil. Analysts tested whether Claude would assist with deceptive campaigning, misinformation, and other forms of election abuse. They began with direct requests, then broke full campaigns into smaller tasks that could look harmless on their own, such as audience research, building news sites, drafting content, and planning its distribution. They found that Claude reliably refused a single harmful request, but could miss a malicious campaign when it was spread across many individual requests that looked harmless on their own.
Building on these findings and our own, we've added new classifiers to better identify novel and multi-step misuse, including attempts to build fake social media accounts and news sites aimed at political discussions, or to run financially motivated election schemes. We also enhanced our ability to detect election-related misuse by foreign state actors, and strengthened our cyber protections for election infrastructure and campaigns. Finally, we built targeted safeguards for localized risks identified in the US, Israel, and Brazil, which all have major national elections this year.
Our threat intelligence and enforcement teams review flagged activity and take action when they confirm a violation, including banning accounts. We also routinely share
examples
of unintended model actions or behavior we've observed during our evaluations and internal use of Claude.
What we've found
Our recent
threat intelligence report
reflects a broader shift in election-related abuse trends. Political, state-aligned, and commercial actors are now incorporating AI into nearly every aspect of their influence operations, from planning and content creation to building platforms used to disseminate a message. Because we see these early stages of an operation happening on Claude, we often have a chance to stop these efforts before they ever reach the public.
Our teams have continued to investigate and prevent coordinated abuse around elections, including the US midterms. In one case, foreign-based operators of a fake news site used Claude to produce US midterm coverage favoring Russian, Iranian, and North Korean narratives. We've also observed threat actors seeking to exploit the election for financial gain, using Claude to produce fabricated news and other content designed to attract American audiences and generate advertising revenue. We banned the accounts involved in these cases and improved our ability to detect this type of abuse.
Looking ahead
More people are turning to Claude for information about this year’s elections than ever before. We have a responsibility to make sure the answers they get are accurate and balanced, and that Claude isn’t used to undermine the democratic process. We’ll continue to invest in making Claude more evenhanded, preventing and addressing misuse, and being transparent in our actions. This work will be critical in the upcoming US midterms and extends to elections around the world as well. In the coming months, we also hope to share a more comprehensive look at how people used Claude throughout the election cycle, with the goal of strengthening our election-related evaluations and safeguards.
Footnotes
We took a random sample of 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026 and analyzed them in a privacy-preserving way.
This figure was generated from a separate analysis of 250,000 Claude.ai conversations, which were reviewed against our election integrity policy.

news.title: An update on independent evaluators
news.content:
Announcements
An update on independent evaluators
Oct 15, 2026
Last month, we committed to
stronger independent, third-party assessment
of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from
METR
, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.
METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on
several reviews of our Risk Reports
. We’re also working with
SecureBio
and
Accenture
as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including
Hugging Face
Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators.
Why we work with independent evaluators
As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.
To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following:
Expertise
in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as
alignment faking
Independence
: they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it.
Enough
access
to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more.
Freedom to publish
observations and assessments
of a model or a process.
Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.
For the AI industry, this is a step toward
robust safety oversight
. We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.
What we mean by “employee-like access”
We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk.
METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into predefined categories like the ones above. (Anthropic ultimately decides what information does and does not fall into these categories, although METR reserves the right to make certain statements about the level of access and information it received.)
Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners.
Our other evaluator partnerships
We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators.
We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions.
In the first tier,
evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval.
In the second tier,
evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified.
The third tier
is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier.
SecureBio
is in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our
August Risk Report
, after completing and
publishing a pilot review
of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access.
With Accenture
and Faculty, we're working
toward an ambitious partnership
that includes evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, testing model safeguards, and building capabilities across our organizations.
We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same.
Footnotes
Because these evaluators (like bank examiners) may also work with other companies, we exercise caution around the possibility of inadvertent leaks. Information about architectures presents a high risk of inadvertent leaks, and its relevance to risk assessment is typically low. When it is highly relevant, we will generally seek to share it, though this will require explicit internal approvals.

news.title: Claude discovers a novel enzyme system with CRISPR-like repeats
news.content:
Science
Claude discovers a novel enzyme system with CRISPR-like repeats
Sep 23, 2026
We’re introducing a new life sciences research group and laboratory at Anthropic. Our focus is on fundamental biology research using Claude: exploring datasets of DNA to identify uncharacterized protein families, generating hypotheses at scale, and testing them through experiments in the lab. This post introduces the team behind this work and shares early results in which Claude discovered a novel enzyme system with properties reminiscent of CRISPR, with only high-level direction from our scientists.
Many discoveries that have revolutionized biology and medicine started with a scientist noticing something odd in the staggering diversity of molecular machines found in nature. Restriction enzymes
proteins that cut DNA at specific short sequences
were found in bacterial immune systems, where they destroy the DNA of invading viruses. Researchers realized they could use these enzymes to cut DNA at chosen places and splice genes from one organism into another, which launched the biotechnology industry. Taq polymerase, an enzyme that copies DNA at high temperatures, was identified in a bacterium in a Yellowstone hot spring. It became the basis for PCR, the DNA-copying method used in much of modern diagnostics. CRISPR was first noticed as an unusual repeat sequence in the DNA of certain bacteria, and is now the foundation of gene editing-based medicines.
In the spring of 2026, we formed a research group to see whether general AI models can systematize and
accelerate such discoveries
. We believe that this acceleration will come from establishing a new way of doing biology research, in which agents collaborate with humans in every step of the process. Developing this new way of working required that we build our own lab and a single team working on everything from training Claude in biology to running experiments in the lab.
Today, we’re sharing early results from one of our first research programs, in which Claude autonomously discovered a novel enzyme system that is associated with an array of DNA repeats, a pattern reminiscent of CRISPR. Although we don’t yet know its function, the system that Claude discovered has a set of characteristics that have only ever been found together in a handful of other systems, all of which are programmable and perform operations like cutting, copying, and pasting DNA. Beyond CRISPR, which has already transformed science and medicine, several other such systems are now in development as promising tools.
The system that Claude found is based on a reverse transcriptase (RT), enzymes that copy RNA into DNA. While this underlying RT, found in a jumbo phage, had been identified in previous studies, Claude appears to be the first to notice the system’s defining features—an associated array of non-coding DNA sequences and an additional accessory protein of unknown function.
After reviewing the pre-print, Feng Zhang, one of the pioneers of CRISPR genome editing and a professor at MIT and the Broad Institute, said:
This is an exciting example of how AI agents can contribute to biological discovery. The identification of RNA-repeat arrays associated with reverse transcriptases is genuinely intriguing and merits further investigation. I hope this work encourages more scientists to explore how AI can support their research.
We gave Claude a prompt to search through a massive database of DNA sequences for interesting new examples of RTs. Our involvement was limited to the initial prompt and the lab work, while Claude agents combed through the database, investigated the distinct RT families, and used their own judgment to identify interesting candidates. After 21 hours spent searching this data by roughly 950 agents using 210 million tokens, one of the agents spotted something remarkable: a repeating pattern of DNA sequences that occurs next to the gene for an odd-looking RT. After further analysis and testing in our lab, we recognized that this pattern marked a previously uncharacterized enzyme system found in bacteriophages (the viruses that infect bacteria) that we call array-associated reverse transcriptases (ART).
Our work to understand the primary function of ARTs is ongoing. However, we think it is important to share such findings early, both to demonstrate Claude’s capabilities and to give the broader community insight into what we’re working on. We have released a pre-print (
here
) that discusses this in more detail.
About our lab
We are a team of scientists who have spent our careers exploring unusual proteins, and specialize in using computational approaches to systematically read DNA, interpret its evolution, and pick out biological systems for further characterization. Our research prior to joining Anthropic has helped to better understand the
evolution
and
regulation
of CRISPR systems, discover new
enzymes
for next-generation
cell and gene therapies
, and build
tools
for accelerating the identification of anomalies in DNA, such as human pathogenic variants. We are part of Anthropic’s life sciences organization, alongside teams whose work includes drug discovery, and training Claude in biology and chemistry.
Our lab, located in the Bay Area, looks like a typical molecular biology lab. We do research that involves only the lower levels of the biosafety risk level (BSL-1 and BSL-2) and we do not handle pathogens that can infect humans. All of the lab work is performed by human scientists. Although we’ve experimented with using AI to accelerate lab work with initiatives like the
Model Hardware Standard
, this approach is less conducive to the sort of ad hoc workflows that are involved in our molecular biology research.
How we work
Many of our workflows involve having Claude search through the vast collection of DNA sequences associated with proteins without a known function. One typical pattern begins with a survey of a given protein family. Claude reads the relevant literature and reproduces the established results from public data to check its methods. It then searches for family members or genomic neighbors that fit no described system, and writes a short, human-readable report for each candidate that proposes a function and describes the evidence supporting its claims. In follow-up analyses, Claude critically evaluates the evidence—typically most candidates are eliminated at this stage. A survey may end with a single candidate worth testing, or with none.
When a candidate survives our review, we test it in the laboratory, expressing the protein in standard laboratory strains and characterizing it biochemically and structurally, with Claude helping to interpret the data. We do our work in
Claude Science
and
Claude Code
, the same tools available to any scientist, and sometimes with a harness of our own that coordinates many Claude sessions running in parallel.
Because Claude produces hypotheses so prolifically, the hypotheses themselves have become an object of study for us. With hundreds to thousands of candidate reports from a single campaign, we have been asking what distinguishes the proposals we judge worth testing from those we set aside. What we learn goes back into the instructions we give Claude and teaches it to mimic our own scientific taste.
Claude finds ART
In the past few years, researchers have discovered many more reverse transcriptases (RTs), most of them in bacteria, where they act as part of the immune system. Nearly all RT families were found by genomic analysis, or genome mining, which requires researchers to search sequence databases for genes that no one has characterized, notice the unusual ones, and work out what they do.
Claude agents gathered over 200,000 RTs, picked out 3,500 new candidate systems, and narrowed those to the 20 most compelling candidates that they analyzed to produce human-readable reports. For an expert scientist, this type of analysis can take weeks to months of work.
During the course of its research, Claude noticed an unusual RT family and decided to examine it in greater detail. While combing through the raw DNA sequence near the RT, the agent exclaimed: “[The DNA next to the RT] is spectacular: I can see by eye a tandem repeat array … that's a CRISPR-like … repeat array?!”
The raw DNA Claude was reading when it detected a repeat pattern that no one had noticed
It then proceeded much as a human scientist would when faced with a potential discovery. It counted the repeats and measured their spacing, compared the layout with the known RT systems, and searched the literature for any previous report of the pattern. After a thorough analysis it was convinced that it had found a new biological system, and filed a report for human review.
The system it found, ART, is found mainly in bacteriophages and consists of three parts: the RT, a partner gene beside it, and a long array of evenly spaced DNA repeat sequences. The repeat layout resembles a CRISPR array, which holds a bank of different RNA sequences that make CRISPR-Cas systems programmable biotechnological tools. Our first experiments show that the ART array is also expressed as a set of distinct short RNAs, suggesting that something analogous may be at play for this system.
Further experiments are underway to determine how ART works, and we are sharing these early findings to show the community that Claude can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses to initiate biological discoveries.
You can find more detail in our technical report (
here
Work with us
We hope this work demonstrates the value of AI-driven hypothesis generation to the wider scientific community, and we would like to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems, in genomics and in other fields. If you have a proposal for a research question, we would like to hear from you.

Today we are removing barriers to government AI adoption by offering Claude for Enterprise and Claude for Government to all three branches of government, including federal civilian executive branch agencies, as well as legislative and judiciary branches of government, for $1.
As AI adoption leads to transformation across industries, we want to ensure that federal workers can fully harness these capabilities to better serve the American people. By removing cost barriers, we're enabling the government to access the same advanced AI that's already proving its value in the private sector.
Government partners are already using Claude to improve and accelerate their work, ranging from groundbreaking scientific breakthroughs to mission-critical national security operations, and we can’t wait for more partners to use Claude's capabilities to advance their missions.

documentation.

Announcements
Oct 14, 2026
Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI.
“We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.”
Supporting responsible AI in Singapore
Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors.
“Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.”
“Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.”
Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the
Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox
run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a
red-teaming project
in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil.
Under the MOU, we plan to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions on model evaluation, testing standards, and incident response. We do similar work with safety institutes around the world, where sharing technical information provides governments with a clearer view of frontier AI capabilities and risks, while helping developers build safer models.
We’ll also look for ways to strengthen AI skills in Singapore, help small and medium-sized businesses adopt AI responsibly, and support the government’s goal of building AI capability among public officers. We plan to share research and data with the government, including from the
, and to offer technical and policy expertise as Singapore develops its rules for AI.
How Singapore is working with Claude
In our latest
Economic Index
, Singapore ranks second of 121 countries in Claude.ai usage relative to its population, at nearly six times what its size alone would predict.
In the public sector, more than 1,500 engineers and technical staff at the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have adopted Claude Code to modernize government systems and speed up software delivery. This has helped GovTech Singapore teams build, maintain, and enhance digital services more efficiently at national scale. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore is exploring how Claude could help strengthen the country’s cyber defense.
In financial services, DBS, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, works with Claude across a range of use cases in its Singapore operations—including software development and day-to-day productivity—as part of its broader AI innovation efforts. These applications operate within the bank’s strict security and governance framework. GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, is rolling out Claude across its investment and corporate services teams. Organizations in regulated sectors like financial services can now run Claude with
in-region inference
on Amazon Bedrock, helping them meet strict data processing requirements.
Singapore’s largest technology companies and startups are building with Claude too. Grab powers BriX, its sales assistant, with Claude. The assistant saves Grab’s sales teams approximately 40,000 hours every quarter and surfaces new sales opportunities. Sea—the business behind Shopee, Garena, and Monee—works with Claude to help Shopee’s customer service chatbot respond faster and more accurately, and thousands of its employees write and debug code with Claude. And Supabase—the developer platform with strong roots in Singapore—is building with Claude Code.
Building with the developer community
This week, senior leaders from Anthropic are in Singapore to open the office and meet with customers, developers, and policymakers.
Today, we hosted Builder Summit Singapore, bringing more than 300 developers together with engineering and product leaders from Anthropic. Earlier in the week, Singapore’s Claude community ambassadors held a meetup for more than 700 local builders.
Our Singapore office is now open and hiring. To learn more about joining the team, visit our

How Notion ships and scales agents with Claude Managed Agents

Case Study: Notion
Learn how Notion uses Claude to power enterprise AI search, reduce costs by 90% with prompt caching, and build agent workflows.
Read more
Three weeks after launching External Agents, collaborative AI workspace Notion had 18,000 agents created by customers, and 90% of agent activity running on automated triggers rather than chat. Notion built the feature on Claude Managed Agents, Anthropic's suite of composable APIs for building and deploying agents at scale. Product manager Eric Liu spoke with Anthropic about what Managed Agents handled and what's surprised him since launch.
Eric Liu, Notion: We want Notion to be the best collaboration platform for agents and teams. A key part of that mission is bringing the best agents to work natively in Notion, and Claude is at the top of that list: the number one external agent people wanted to use in Notion. So far it's about 18,000 Claude agents created, and those agents have done about 140,000 steps. We were pleasantly surprised by how quickly it ramped up, with very little marketing. A large percentage of people creating agents in Notion now create Claude agents. We're seeing strong depth of usage too. 90% of the turns people are doing with Claude are automations in Notion, triggered on a Notion page, a Slack message, or scheduled runs. It's not directly chatting with Claude; the wrapper we built around it for automations is what's resonating with our customers. Our top workspaces are really using it for multiplayer workflows: a workspace will have three or four agents running dozens of threads per day, mainly through automations.
Liu: You’re creating these software building blocks in Notion and you can construct them into any workflow you want. For example, we created a task board that acts as an orchestrator. You create a task, move it to "ready to start," and it invokes a Claude session. Claude picks up context from connected pages, our design system, API docs, and product requirements documents. In other words, you're working with Claude just like a colleague.
The nice thing is that you're not limited to one task. Customers can kick off 30 or 40 jobs at the same time, and our platform routes them to the right person for approvals. People are automating the busy work: experiment flag cleanup, a lot of different mini tasks around triage.
"Claude is the number one external agent people wanted to use in Notion."
Eric Liu
Product Manager, Notion
Liu: Users were asking us for Claude. Our customers don't want to use one agent to talk to another agent to do a backflip to get things connected. They just want to be in Notion and say, "Claude, help me make this website." Managed Agents was a great solution because we just pulled in the API and it worked within the product.
We focus on what's native to Notion: your company knowledge. Our agent is good at using Notion, but it's not the best at coding, and Claude models are very good at that. There's a whole world of other files that Claude is really good at generating. Underneath, all agents are basically coding agents. And that's unlocking a lot of non-coding use cases. If you're creating a presentation for marketing or sales, you're taking knowledge and generating an artifact, whether that's a PDF, slides, or something else. That synthesis of information into an artifact is roughly the same workflow that works really well in coding. We're seeing that transition into the rest of knowledge work.
Liu: Our vision with Notion is to make it the command center for agents: allowing teams to use their favorite agent and use it natively within Notion. If you are a collaboration product, the idea of being able to use an agent in the product is the core user journey. The benefit of bringing in Claude is people trust the intelligence of the model and the experience.
The session streams from Managed Agents into Notion's client. But to the user, they don't know any of that is happening. All they're seeing is that Claude is writing files, writing Notion pages, updating things, commenting and doing everything that teammates and other agents can do.
Liu: Having an infrastructure layer that can do long-running tasks was really essential. That ability to continue to run tasks, to manage memory, and to have high quality outputs over time is a layer that's super critical on top of the model itself.
The best surprise was that we didn't have to set up any of this. All of the skills, all the different packages we need, it was very easy to go and spin up.
The sandbox is really important if you want coding use cases. Part of our flow for users is the ability to connect their GitHub, and through that they can pull in their repos and then run the code. The GitHub endpoint in Managed Agents was really useful.
Liu: The challenge of deploying agents at scale is really about collaboration. Right now, agents feel very one-to-one. It's you and an agent in an interface. But what does it look like for your whole team, with all of the approval processes and everything required to actually use agents at scale? That's fundamentally the same problem we've solved before at Notion, which is human collaboration. Now it's agent and human collaboration, and it turns out a lot of the same patterns around suggested edits, version history, and shared knowledge bases are really critical.
Liu: The Managed Agents product is like a playground for me. Even with the early prototype, we saw 12 hours of prototyping work collapse into about 20 minutes. Then your whole team can jump in and refine it together.
When I was prototyping new features for Notion using the task board workflow, I had about 30 tasks. I took all of them and just dragged them to start. I went and got a snack, came back, and all the prototypes were made. Then I tagged in somebody on my team, and we jammed on the same output together right in Notion. We've turned AI solo work into a collaborative moment. That was the point where I was like, everybody should be doing this.
People now see Claude show up in their Notion task doing work, and they give a thumbs up or thumbs down. That's an interface they already understand.
Liu: We've created a Claude agent for each stage: one that investigates, one that plans, and one that builds. What's useful about that is each agent can have its own permissions, its own contexts, and its own automations. The review agent is managed by a few people, but many people can manage the investigator agent.
Every agent that you create is locked down from a permission standpoint by default, which means it starts private. You have to share it explicitly. Then we have a bunch of different access permissions: some people will only be able to chat with it, some people can trigger it, some people can edit it. When you have 20 or 30 people working on the same shared task board, how do you make sure that at the right point, the right person is brought in? The way that we think about solving the automated workflow is also solving the permissions and collaboration problems. Those go hand in hand.
Claude Managed Agents: Get to production 10x faster
We're launching Claude Managed Agents, a suite of composable APIs for building and deploying cloud-hosted agents at scale.
Read more
"The benefit of bringing in Claude is people trust the intelligence of the model and the experience."
Eric Liu
Product Manager, Notion
Liu: Claude has a lot of great skills, so we preloaded the ones that are publicly available for making PowerPoints, PDFs, and docs. Within Notion, we have a whole marketplace of skills, and we're letting folks bring in their own skills for their own Claude agent.
With skills, it's more about how you do something, and not so much if it can do it. It’s not about knowing how to make a PowerPoint, but more about "Hey, this is our flavor of PowerPoint. This is how we like it written."
A lot of these skills are basically auto-maintained. Once there's a merged pull request or a completed task, Claude identifies the lessons the agent can learn and feeds them back into the skills as updates. Every time you say "this is a great prototype" or "this is a great PDF," that feeds into the skills. The quality keeps improving without someone manually updating the knowledge base.
Liu: The interface is becoming more about human beings reviewing the work of agents. We are the translation layer to agents. We'll keep the same primitives around the page and the database, but we're going to build a lot more around version control and humans in the loop.
The question becomes: how can humans become the reviewers of agentic work rather than directly the doers? I think that paradigm applies to a lot of AI.

Figma recognized that the role of design is rapidly evolving with AI. As the leading design platform, they saw an opportunity to help designers expand their creative impact—enabling them to bring designs to life—while inviting more people into the design process.
AI unlocks a new way to quickly visualize design ideas and turn static mocks into interactive experiences with a simple prompt. By bringing this capability to Figma, teams can explore many different directions without manually creating prototypes or writing code.
This evolution also aligned with broader industry shifts. Alex Mullans, a product manager at Figma, noted, "The traditional handoff between design and development creates friction. There's back-and-forth where the developer returns saying 'here's what I built,' and it doesn't match the original vision.” Figma’s collaborative platform brings design and development closer together to maintain craft and quality throughout the entire process.
Choosing Claude for technical prowess and design sensibility
When evaluating AI models, Figma sought a solution that could generate high-quality code while understanding design intent and aesthetics.
Mullans described their evaluation process, saying, "We regularly evaluate various models. Claude consistently delivers the right combination of speed, accuracy, and understanding user intent."
Claude's design sensibility also sets it apart, the team shared. An engineer for Figma Make explained: "Before Anthropic came around, you saw these AI models were intelligent, but they definitely lacked taste, they lacked character. You would ask them to generate a design and the design would come out rather flat. And then Anthropic came around and now we have both intelligent models and models with taste."
Holly Li, product manager for Figma Make, had firsthand experience with Claude's capabilities. "I spent 30 hours teaching myself React to build my website. With Claude, I refactored and improved all that code in a single day, adding features I'd always wanted but couldn't implement myself."
The team identified Claude Sonnet as their breakthrough moment—the point when code generation became good enough to enable their vision for Figma Make.
Alex Mullans, a product manager at Figma
Interactivity via natural language
Figma integrated Claude into two transformative products that turn ideas into code-backed software. The first allows designers working in Figma Sites to add interactivity to existing website designs by describing what they want—selecting elements and typing natural language prompts like "add a hover effect that tilts when my mouse is over it." Claude quickly generates high-quality code while preserving the details of the original design.
The second product, Figma Make, creates interactive prototypes or apps from descriptions or existing Figma designs. As Li explained: "Figma Make is a way to go from idea to real software. You can either start from scratch or start with an existing design that you've created in Figma." Users can type a prompt describing what they want, or copy their pixel-perfect mockups from Figma Design, and Claude transforms them into fully functional prototypes with complex logic, animations, and responsive behaviors.
Li articulated their design philosophy, saying, "AI should meet designers where they are. If you've already crafted the perfect design, you shouldn't have to start over. Claude adds the interactivity while respecting every pixel you've placed."
The team saw remarkable improvements with each Claude update. Li shared, "A prompt now generates sophisticated designs with gradients, varied typography, and thoughtful motion. One of our designers even said 'Claude is so good, I want to cry.'"
New models accelerate the vision
The Figma team stays on the cutting edge, constantly testing the latest Claude models.
"Sonnet 4.5 is a very impressive model," said Dylan Field, Figma CEO. "We're very impressed so far with how much it can plan ahead, and also how much it can reason about complex codebases." Field explained how the model has transformed Figma designs into functional code. He highlighted the improved round-trip workflow between Figma Design and Make—copying designs in, generating working prototypes, then bringing them into the design canvas to iterate further and compare explorations side-by-side. "We had no idea how much better this round trip would get with Sonnet 4.5... it's been a very happy surprise," he noted. Field called the experience "a joy to play with," adding that the model "has already really shown quite a difference" in Figma Make's capabilities.
Figma also introduced an experimental models setting, giving users access to the latest releases—including the new Claude Opus 4.6—as soon as they're available in Figma Make. "Claude Opus 4.6 generates complex, interactive apps and prototypes in Figma Make with an impressive creative range," said Loredana Crisan, Chief Design Officer at Figma. "The model translates detailed designs and multi-layered tasks into code on the first try, making it a powerful starting point for teams to explore and build ideas." The experimental setting lets teams push the boundaries with new capabilities as Claude continues to evolve.
Every new model release unlocks new possibilities for what teams can create. Field shared, “As AI models get better, Figma gets better.”
Making design and software creation accessible to everyone
By lowering technical barriers, Claude enables all kinds of Figma users to validate ideas faster, explore more creative directions, and bring diverse perspectives into the product development process.
Speed transforms what's possible. Li illustrated this with her own experience, saying, "I prototyped a new product flow with Figma Make in five minutes. Before, that would have been literally impossible for me to do alone as a product manager without design and engineering support."
This acceleration enables entirely new workflows. Early users have shared compelling examples: one designer pitched a VC on a startup idea by prototyping it over a weekend using Figma Make, impressing the investor with a fully functional demo. Another user used Make to bring a long-shelved concept to life—turning it interactive finally got the company talking about it again.
Beyond individual productivity, Claude also democratizes who can contribute to product development. Mullans observed, "Product managers who think in spreadsheets and data tables can now create visual prototypes to communicate their ideas. Engineers can quickly mock up interfaces without spending time with CSS. Everyone across the organization can contribute more effectively to the design process."
The shift goes deeper than tools—it's changing how teams approach product development. Now, engineers can design, product managers can prototype, and designers can ship software. Figma Make is blurring the boundaries between different roles, helping everyone visualize an idea, participate in the design process, and bring a product to life.
"Claude Opus 4.6 generates complex, interactive apps and prototypes in Figma Make with an impressive creative range."

Zendesk built custom agents on Claude and reached 1 million agent executions in 7 weeks

1 million custom agent executions
in the first seven weeks of early access

in human handle times for customers running custom agents
Zendesk, which provides AI for customer and employee service, built a way for its customers to create their own AI agents for the parts of their service work that are specific to their business. The agents run on Claude, and they ran 1 million times in their first seven weeks of early access.
With Claude, Zendesk:
Built its custom agent builder with a five-person team, working with Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK, going from proof of concept to early access in four months
Went from zero to 1 million custom agent executions within seven weeks of early access
Helped one customer that handles more than 14 million service requests a year automate duplicate merging at 99% accuracy in its pilot
Raised automated resolution by up to 10% while cutting human handle times by up to 80% for customers running custom agents
Runs Claude through Amazon Bedrock, inside the AWS environment and hosting regions it already operates
The challenge
The work that stayed manual
Zendesk already helps companies automate a large share of their customer requests with AI. The harder part is the work that happens between a customer’s first message and the final outcome, like exceptions to a return policy, complicated warranty claims, or detailed billing questions.
Smaller companies handled that work with people, one request at a time. Larger ones with AI teams built one-off automations, which took a lot of engineering time and only covered the easiest cases. “Every customer is so unique to what they do,” said Abhinay Kathuria, Director of AI/ML at Zendesk. “There’s a lot that happens behind-the-scenes, and a lot of this was being handled manually.”
The solution
Powering custom agents with Claude Sonnet
Kathuria’s team tested models from Anthropic and other providers on the testing system they use across Zendesk products. It scores each model on 15 metrics using agents like the ones customers actually write, and the team runs it again whenever a new model comes out. Because these agents act on real customer requests, getting the answer right matters a lot.
Zendesk chose Claude Sonnet 4.6. Sonnet did “exceedingly well” on pilot tasks like reading PDFs, and in Zendesk’s testing, it needed fewer steps to reach a decision. “A competitor model might come to the same conclusion, but it might take four or five planning turns to get there,” Kathuria said. “Sonnet could handle a lot of those in one shot.”
Kathuria now makes the same argument to Zendesk customers. “You can’t just look at token price in isolation,” he said. “You have to look at the cost per task.”
Where Claude runs came down to security and data locality. Zendesk already runs its infrastructure on Amazon Web Services (AWS), so it serves Claude through Amazon Bedrock. Zendesk keeps model processing in the AWS hosting regions it already uses, which helps it meet customers’ data-residency and governance requirements. Zendesk says this also means its customers don’t have to approve or manage an additional cloud subprocessor. “Our most important security benefit is that Claude runs through the AWS environment we already operate and govern,” Kathuria shares.
Agents written in English, connected to the tools teams already have
To set up a custom agent, a Zendesk customer writes instructions in plain English, then connects the agent to Zendesk actions and outside tools like Jira and Google Drive in a few clicks. It takes about 30 minutes to set up something that used to take months of engineering work.
Take incident triage. When a lot of similar tickets come in at once, the agent notices, files a Jira issue, posts in Slack to let engineers know, and tells the affected customers the problem is being worked on. Once the fix ships, it closes all the related tickets and adds a note explaining what went wrong.
Zendesk is also building a router to send each task to the right place. Simple requests, like working out what a customer is asking for, take one call to Sonnet. Harder ones go through a longer process where the agent plans its steps before acting. After each run, the agent reviews its own work and saves what it learned as a skill it can use next time.
Customers decide which actions each agent is allowed to take. Zendesk is also shipping ways to watch and test agents, including a log of every tool call, simulated conversations, and A/B testing. “Our customers are asking for exactly the same things we need internally,” Kathuria said. “A lot more agent observability, and how to test these agents in production.”
“Our most important security benefit is that Claude runs through the AWS environment we already operate and govern,”
Abhinay Kathuria
Director of AI/ML, Zendesk
The outcome
1 million agent executions in seven weeks
In the first seven weeks of early access, custom agents ran 1 million times. General availability is planned for Zendesk's AI Summit in November and several large customers are getting ready to move much more volume onto them. “We have four or five customers who are going to run 20 million tickets through these agents powered by Claude every year,” Kathuria said.
Across customers running custom agents, automated resolution has gone up by as much as 10%. Zendesk calls its long-term goal an Autonomous Service Workforce, where AI handles 80% or more of customer and employee requests and people handle the rest with help from AI. Next, it plans to offer more specialized agents built for specific industries and types of work.
“The era of generic, one-size-fits-all AI agents is over. The best agents are specialists: deeply grounded in the work, the industry, and the business they serve,” said Shashi Upadhyay, President of Product, Engineering and AI at Zendesk. “Our custom agents powered by Claude are taking on more complex work, earning trust, and driving more measurable impact for our customers.”
“Our custom agents powered by Claude are taking on more complex work, earning trust, and driving more measurable impact for our customers.”
Shashi Upadhyay
President of Product, Engineering and AI, Zendesk
